entries.title: Earth’s Condition Is ‘Serious and Getting Worse’ as Climate Change Intensifies
entries.summary: Seven of 16 planetary vital signs are in their most extreme state ever recorded, and El Niño is here to make matters even worse.
entries.content:
The climate just got its annual checkup, and the results aren’t looking so hot.

“If Earth were a patient coming in for an annual physical, I would say its condition is serious and getting worse,” Oregon State University researcher Bill Ripple says.

Ripple is the lead author of a new paper chronicling the state of the climate, published on Wednesday in BioScience. The findings show that seven of the 16 planetary vital signs tracked by the researchers have never been in a more extreme state.

That includes the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which is 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels due to burning fossil fuels, as well as symptoms of burning all that oil, coal, and gas. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have shrunk to record lows, while ocean heat has soared to record highs.

Climate change has already quickened the pace of warming from about 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade from 1880 through 1970 to 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade since 2010, according to the analysis. While the global average temperature, including land, isn’t at a record extreme, that may change by the end of the year as El Niño strengthens. The natural climate pattern is characterized by a hotter-than-normal Pacific Ocean, but it also boosts global heat levels by pouring more energy into the atmosphere. This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be one for the record books.

“A strong El Niño could temporarily push global temperatures even higher, while bringing additional heat and drought to vulnerable regions,” says Ripple. He adds that “El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it's now occurring on top of a much warmer planet. That makes its impacts potentially more dangerous.”

Of particular concern are ecosystems such as coral reefs and tropical forests. The spread of ocean heat is likely to fuel a mass coral die-off, known as coral bleaching. With each successive wave of bleaching, reefs become less resilient. Corals are among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change; if the planet warms beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, most of the world’s coral will be unlikely to survive.

Tropical forests also face pressure from El Niño. This is especially true of the Amazon, which tends to see dry weather during this climate pattern. The timing couldn’t be more dire: The region, dubbed “the world’s lungs,” is already under intense pressure from logging and mining interests and the possible return of a right-wing government in Brazil that prioritizes extraction and land clearing over conservation.

The new report also warns that the Amazon is among the ecosystems at risk of crossing a tipping point—that is, reaching a threshold where it shifts from a tropical rainforest into something more resembling savanna. It’s highly unlikely that crossing that tipping point is imminent, let alone something that will happen this year. But this year’s blast of El Niño–influenced weather will edge it closer.

“Warming, drought, and deforestation could push the Amazon toward widespread forest degradation,” Ripple says. “My concern is that these changes could interact, making them increasingly difficult to stop.”

The report is an avalanche of bad news for the climate, though it does note that carbon-free forms of energy are playing a bigger role in the power grid. The report calls it a sign we’re in the “Age of Electricity.” Despite that, annual greenhouse gas emissions are at record highs. In other words, the world is still smoking a pack a day, even at the risk of losing a lung.

“There are some encouraging signs, especially the growth of renewable energy, but they aren't yet enough to reverse the overall deterioration,” Ripple says. “The climate emergency is not something waiting for us in the future. We are already living through it.”

entries.title: ‘Dune: Part Three’ Cowriter Brian K. Vaughan Has a New Comic on the Way
entries.summary: Brian K. Vaughan claims he’s seen Dune: Part Three and it’s “a fucking beautiful movie.”
entries.content:
Brian K. Vaughan would like to apologize. He knows everyone is dying for details about Dune: Part Three, which he cowrote with director Denis Villeneuve, but his lips are pretty sealed until December 18 when the film finally hits theaters.

“Sorry to be coy,” he says as we’re about to leave the New York coffee shop where we’ve been chatting. “I hope the day will come where I’m able to say much, much more. It was truly so awesome. I can’t believe it happened.”

Vaughan is in the city for New York Comic Con, but not to talk about Dune. Ostensibly, he came to the convention to talk about Paper Girls, the comic he created with Cliff Chiang that was turned into a 2022 Amazon Prime Video series. During the Paper Girls panel, however, the pair announced that they’re working on a new comic, Roam, a superhero sci-fi series set to come out in February of next year.

Roam, Vaughan tells me, came from a deep desire to work with Chiang again. They’d considered doing a short eight-page story or maybe a one-shot, but eventually they said “Fuck it. Let’s do an ongoing series.”

Vaughan has the kind of career writers of a certain ilk would kill for. He started working on comics in the 1990s and has been the pen behind favorites like Saga, Y: The Last Man, and Marvel’s Runaways. (Those last two got turned into TV series; the outlier, Saga, is a story people have wanted to see adapted for years.) He also served as a writer on Lost and created CBS’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Under the Dome.

Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”

Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.

On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:

It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.

I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.

On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:

It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.

I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?

In Roam there's an element of this as well; AI is a component in the story. So, it's something I guess I need to write about with my human meat machine to process, but I'm in the middle of thinking about it, as you are, every day.

OK, a little bit about Dune: Part Three, which he has seen:

I can't say very much other than it’s a tremendous, insane, ridiculous honor to be involved with it, and my contributions are modest. Denis’ true cowriter on this is Frank Herbert. The novel is the star. And it's obviously the greatest cast and crew ever assembled. It's a fucking beautiful movie. It's my favorite of the three. which I can say with genuine humility. I can't say anything other than it's just as wonderful as you can imagine.

I got special thanks in the first movie. I was doing a tiny amount of consulting. I was working at Legendary [the media company that owns the rights to Dune] at the time, and they just invited me in to see an early cut, which was as fantastic as the finished product. But I just ended up talking to Denis, honestly. Never before has a director been that talented, also that decent and warm as a human being. I wasn't anticipating getting this call at the beginning of three, but it's obviously a call I could not refuse.

I should probably just be discreet at this point. The movie doesn't need me to promote it. I'm reluctant to do anything that makes me sound more important to this process.

On the future of Hollywood:

I am a small worker in the world of Hollywood. It is changing so rapidly that who knows what it's gonna be like tomorrow, six months from now.

But again, I've got teenagers and I see how delighted they were by Backrooms, by Obsession. It feels like Gen X has been force-feeding them a lot of my childhood stories that we have gussied up, and they are clearly hungry for something new.

On why he doesn’t write adaptations of his own comics:

I've taken stabs at it in the past. Richard Price, the novelist, I once heard him say in response to “Why don't you adapt your own stuff more?” that adapting your own work is like being a dentist and giving yourself a root canal. Just because you can do it, doesn't mean you should. Let some other motherfucker handle that. I believe those were Mr. Price's words.

It's been constructive and a thrill to adapt other people, and I like getting to watch other people adapt me, but I've also been doing a lot of it for the last decade, where it feels like I've either been adapting or being adapted. I think that was part of the siren song of Roam. It’s time to break some new ground.

Denis says that to adapt something you love is to do violence to it. When I've been adapted, that has always been what I've told people. It is much more important for this to be good than to be faithful. He's a master of cinema, and cinema is rarely about people sitting in a room having dialog. How do you transliterate this to cinema? That's an alchemy that I don't understand. He's just unparalleled at that.

On Lost and why writing for commercial breaks was a challenge:

I love my prestige drama without commercials, but there was a degree of difficulty working on Lost and having a cliff-hanger five times an episode. To have that was such a challenge and so rewarding when you were able to pull it off. Can you write something where people are like, “OK, I'll just wet my pants. I cannot risk not coming back [before the break is over].”

entries.title: Formlabs Has a 3D Printer for Normies
entries.summary: The Form Studio 1 is a $699 desktop-sized printer that fits on a desk and only stinks a little bit.
entries.content:
Fourteen boxes are piled in front of my desk, stacked around me like a cardboard fort. Inside one is a Form Studio 1, the new, affordable, consumer-focused 3D printer Formlabs just announced.

David Lakatos, chief product officer at the 3D printer manufacturer, assured me that the Form Studio 1 has a very economical size. “It doesn't take a lot of space,” Lakatos said. “If you have a desk, then I think you should be good to go.” I have a desk. It’s covered in boxes sent by his company.

Formlabs is one of the biggest 3D printer producers, with nearly 200,000 printers in service. The company’s customers are primarily professional businesses, like assembly shops or dentists, able to shell out $2,500 or more for a printer. (Its last affordable printer was $2,300.)

But the Form Studio 1 is Formlabs’ first consumer-oriented device. It prints with SLA (stereolithography) resins—a common 3D printing material that hardens into solid plastic when exposed to ultraviolet light—and can use Formlabs-branded products or third-party resins. It costs $699 and is now on sale; individual resin bottles start at $29.

The Studio 1 takes up roughly the same space as a minifridge. You’ll also likely need a wash unit, sold separately for $199 with a similar footprint (it removes uncured liquid resin from the surface of models). Then you’ll need room for all the tools and resin cartridges. Getting all that stuff can pile up. Or at least it did when Formlabs sent more than a dozen boxes to the WIRED office for testing. Your pileage may vary.

The front touchscreen lets you troubleshoot and ready prints. When the printer starts, it’s relatively quiet and odor-free. 3D printing with resin can be stinky, but Formlabs-branded resins are UL GreenGuard–certified, the same standard used to ensure baby products aren’t harmful from skin contact or off-gassing. Lakatos says the idea is that the Studio 1 can be used anywhere without the room being overwhelmed by resin stank.

“We know that some people are going to put it in their bedrooms,” Lakatos says. “I don't sleep with my printers, but you could if you really wanted to.”

After going through the stack of boxes, I set up the Form Studio 1 and the Form Studio Wash+Cure. They’re stylish, with translucent orange cases that conjure old-school iMac aesthetics. The printing process itself is supposedly quick. Lakatos says you can print a casing for a Raspberry Pi setup in around eight minutes.

I’ve only printed a couple of things so far, but have had a good experience with the orders. (Full review coming soon.) I printed a clear cover for the toolbox that comes with the Studio 1. It took about 17 minutes and came out clean and intact. The process was relatively quiet. The resin smell was there, but really only when lifting the hood after the process was done. I’m excited to use it more and see what kind of very detailed unholy abominations I can make.

The SLA printing enables very detailed constructions. In Formlabs’ internal testing, the company says it has had a roughly 2 percent failure rate for its prints. If that holds in the real world, it’ll be a big jump over competitors. That’s if you use its own resins, though.

“You can use any material,” Lakatos says. “If you want to use the toxic resin on Amazon, you can do it. We don't recommend it, but you can do it.”

Formlabs also has an app called Form Mobile that can control prints or send designs to the Form Studio 1. The overall printer experience feels surprisingly straightforward.

“It’s great if you want to mess around with some stuff,” Lakatos says. “For serious, beautiful things and projects that really require better material properties, beautiful resolution, stuff like that—it's hard to compete with it.”

entries.title: My Friend Has No Soul
entries.summary: The second iteration of the viral Friend AI necklace is louder and less interesting.
entries.content:
My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.

I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.

“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”

“OK, great,” I say.

“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”

“Please stop,” I plead.

“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”

You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.

“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”

Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.

The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.

The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.

It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.

When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.

Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.

I dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.

When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”

“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”

Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.

I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.

“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”

It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.

That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.

"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."

The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.

"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”

“You building God now, huh?” I texted him.

“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.

entries.title: Breville Eye Q Toaster Review: Neat Sensors, but Less-Than-Perfect Toast
entries.summary: The Breville Eye Q uses optical sensors to measure the darkness of your toast. Cool tech, but the toasting quality needs improvement.
entries.content:
It's also pretty good looking as countertop appliances go, a bar that Breville's products tend to clear easily. The “dark noir” brushed steel is handsome, the controls intuitive, and the ceramic-coated top is clean and will likely stay that way over time, more so than a traditional stainless top.

Over the summer, I brought the Eye Q along for a couple of weeks of family time in New Hampshire, where we were often eight or more around the table, tweens to octogenarians. Most everyone was intrigued by the toaster, and encouragingly, nobody needed coaching on how to use it.

During the months I had it, it almost always did an acceptable job. It wasn't hard to get the toast right, but—and this is a big but—compared to a regular toaster, the quality of the toast it made was comparable, not superior. To generalize, especially if you compared front to back on a slice, or piece to piece, the Eye Q's toasting was a little uneven and the top of the toast tended to come out darker than the bottom. A noticeable thing, but nothing a polite person would complain about if you set a couple buttery slices in front of them.

On BLT day, I took my nephew Eli on as intern for the afternoon and had him toast seven consecutively darker batches of toast, one per setting, then line them up in order on a sheet pan. The lowest setting was very light, settings two and three were pretty identical, settings four and five were excellent, setting six was mysteriously lighter than setting four, and setting seven was very dark and a little burnt. Two-slot toasters aren't designed for seven back-to-back cycles of toasting, but it did well enough. Store-bought bagels didn't fare particularly well.

Back in Seattle, I unpacked a new Eye Q, and that one had a bad habit of making lighter shades darker than most people would appreciate, so Breville sent another one along to close out the testing. It worked fine, though it tended to get the edges a little toastier than the center; this seemed to be getting worse as testing wound down, so if you’re thinking about buying one of these, perhaps watch the comments for a couple months before pulling the trigger.

entries.title: The Politics of Solar Energy Are Getting Weird, Mean, and a Little MAGA
entries.summary: A mysterious super PAC that doubles as a pro-solar-energy outfit is funding some of the most knives-out attack ads of the midterms season.
entries.content:
A mysteriously named political action committee has started running ads reminding voters in Colorado about that time GOP representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado and her date were caught on camera in 2023 getting handsy during a performance of the musical Beetlejuice.

That same PAC is producing a spot hitting Anthony Constantino, a Trumpist congressional candidate in upstate New York, because someone used his sticker-printing company to briefly make stickers that read, “Kill the Police.”

Attack ads are everywhere in the last month ahead of November’s election. But these spots are a little different. The semi-anonymous PAC that’s funding and making the ads, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, is a pro-solar-energy outfit. It’s funded in part by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and run by a team of New York City political operatives.

“Playing hardball politics, that's what our opponents do, right, in oil and gas? And I just think the solar industry has been—I don't know how to describe it—a little too nice,” says Larsen, the cofounder of the blockchain finance firm Ripple and a major backer of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.

Green groups don’t usually act like this, with knives out, ready to stab opponents between the ribs. They tend to make appeals based on scientific consensus, or fears of what will happen to a warming planet without collective action. They’re also traditionally Democratic, but a few high-profile members of the MAGA movement are now speaking up for solar too. Texas, the home of the fossil fuel business, has quickly become a solar powerhouse. There are some signs that the Trump administration’s across-the-board opposition to solar may be starting to crack, at least a little, after years of slashing greentech subsidies and throwing up one roadblock after another to clean power projects.

Some of Larsen’s natural allies in the renewables field aren’t too happy about the PAC’s efforts, arguing that they’re alienating the decisionmakers they need most. But the politics of energy, especially solar energy, are changing.

Larsen’s PAC is devoting $15 million to go after seven of the more prominent opponents of renewable energy in this year’s congressional elections. That’s on top of roughly $5 million they’ve already spent in the primaries, cutting ads against Republican representatives Ralph Norman of South Carolina (whom the PAC called a “MAGA traitor”), Andy Ogles of Tennessee (“He doesn’t even bother going to work”), and Chip Roy (“chosen the side of powerful pedophiles”) of Texas. A PAC that received funding from Invest in Tomorrow has also gone after one Democrat, Rhode Island governor Dan McKee. All four lost their primary races.

In Roy’s case, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition spent almost $1.5 million to stop his run for Texas attorney general. Most of the money went to ads on right-wing platforms like Truth Social and Rumble. The word “solar” was never mentioned.

“Don't talk about renewables. Don't talk about climate,” says Chris Coffey, the chief executive of the consultancy Tusk Strategies, which is running the PAC. “Pick the best issue that we can pick. And in a Republican primary, we should savage this guy for not being MAGA enough.”

Roy received a 100 percent rating from Heritage Action, the political arm of the Trumpist think tank. Coffey said he got some pushback from a few Democratic operatives, who were concerned that replacements for Roy and other PAC targets might not be any less extreme—on climate or any other issue. Without their far-right track record, the argument went, those replacements might even be stronger candidates in the general election.

“Who fucking cares? Who cares? Like, it can't be worse,” Coffey, a veteran of New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg’s City Hall, says in response. “At least we'll have extracted some payback.”

The PAC is currently putting $2 million into ads blasting GOP representative Victoria Spartz of Indiana as allegedly corrupt; it’s aiming to target Texas Republican Brandon Herrera for his “abolish old people” jokes and his plan to get rid of Social Security. Then there is the $1.5 million ad campaign about Boebert and the Beetlejuice incident. “If Lauren Boebert can’t be trusted in a room full of kids, then she can’t be trusted in the halls of Congress,” the commercial’s narrator says.

Other special-interest organizations have been running this playbook for decades. Groups supporting labor and opposing gun regulations regularly try to make examples of politicians who oppose their agenda. Green groups haven’t been as aggressive historically. That’s a problem, says Steph Bosh, the board chair of the Community Clean Energy Coalition. While her group has raised nearly $2 million to promote their favored hyperlocal candidates this cycle—and the League of Conservation Voters’ affiliated super PAC is spending another $50 million—Bosh says she appreciates that someone else is taking a less friendly approach.

“As a broad renewable energy industry, we need to be loved, respected, and feared,” Bosh adds. “We need to have a carrot, and we need to have a stick.”

James Carville, the Democratic pundit and former campaign manager, doubts the stick is big enough. “Twenty million—what the fuck do you think the carbon industry spends in a year?” he recently said to the Washington Monthly.

Roy, for his part, insisted that the PAC’s spending had played “zero role” in his race (while his campaign staff put out statements denouncing the “radical California Marxists trying to buy Texas elections”). Ralph Norman, his fellow solar target, warned about the “elite” taking out “the $1 million attack ad against me,” while Ogles complained, “they literally are trying to make an example out of me.”

“They were the difference maker,” Chris Burger, a Republican political consultant in Tennessee, says of the pro-solar group. “I don't think Charlie [Hatcher, Ogles’ primary opponent] wins if the PAC doesn't come in with $2 million.”

The Trump White House and its allies in Congress have been beyond hostile to renewables, which they believe to be intermittent sources of energy, and dominated by China. The administration has done everything it can to promote the production of oil, gas, and coal, while kneecapping renewable alternatives, from tying green projects in bureaucratic knots to pulling billions of dollars’ worth of solar subsidies and paying companies billions more to stop offshore wind farm construction. Then the Trump team tried to get other countries to adopt similar attitudes. “If you don’t get away from the green energy scam, your country is going to fail,” the president told the United Nations General Assembly last year.

But the Trumpists have been slightly less hostile to solar than to offshore wind farms, which, according to the president, cause cancer, “kill all your birds,” and drive whales “crazy.”

“While wind is dead, solar is merely in the ICU,” Richard Goldberg, a former member of the administration's National Energy Dominance Council, tells WIRED.

That has provided a small but real opening to promote solar to the America First set, especially with energy prices spiking at home, the war in Iran pushing up oil prices around the world, and the spread of AI data centers creating a borderline-insatiable need for more power.

In February, the American Clean Power Association launched a campaign to do just that, releasing a poll from former Trump campaign manager Kellyanne Conway’s consulting company showing that 75 percent of MAGA voters in key states supported the idea of adding more solar energy to the national mix. According to an internal memo reviewed by Politico, soon to follow were “paid media partnerships with podcasts like the Katie Miller Pod” (hosted by the former DOGE spokesperson, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller) as well as “advertorials and sponsorships with right-of-center publications.”

Katie Miller, once a consultant for Elon Musk, a renewable energy advocate, has repeatedly pushed for solar on social media since then. “Over 70 percent of the new utility-scale capacity went into states won by President Trump,” reads one of her posts. “Electricity generation is a national security issue—not a partisan one.” (Miller, who did not respond to requests to comment for this story, has previously denied receiving any funding from the clean power group.)

There’s also the data center issue. China hasn’t had problems powering its data centers, thanks in part to its widespread deployment of renewables—315 gigawatts of solar added to the grid last year, about six times more than the United States added from all sources combined. The US is in an entirely different situation. MAGA-minded promoters of solar are trying to leverage that gap to make a Trumpy argument for renewable energy. Concerns about the climate are out; fears about losing the AI race to China are in.

T1 Energy, which bills itself as one of the few truly all-American solar manufacturing companies, has hired Checkmate Government Relations, a lobbying firm led by Donald Trump Jr.’s old hunting buddy, and Tower Strategy, helmed by a former CIA operations officer, Rick De La Torre, to press its case in the administration. These lobbyists have tried to make the case that the administration’s beef isn’t with solar in general; it’s with Chinese solar. They’ve done it in the kind of pec-flexing language that’s become MAGA’s stock-in-trade.

“American-made, utility-scale solar is one of the few technologies that can be deployed at the speed and scale required” for data centers, De La Torre posted on LinkedIn. “China knows this. That is why it continues to flood markets, compress margins, and keep U.S. manufacturers on the defensive. Undercut. Outscale. Outlast.”

“Washington has a choice. Treat solar manufacturing as a strategic industry, the way we now treat semiconductors and critical minerals,” he added. Or only claim “to compete with Beijing.”

There are some indications that the argument may be gaining traction. In August, the Trump administration added a new 15 percent tariff and price floors on foreign-made solar components. T1’s CEO hailed it as a victory for domestic supply chains and manufacturing. More recently, negotiations in Congress are continuing on a bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among many other things, make it easier for solar providers to plug into the electric grid.

Which led some solar executives to question whether it’s smart for the group to beat up on Republicans, right as a few of them seem to be creeping in solar’s direction.

“We’ve been hard at work speaking to Republicans about why supporting solar and batteries helps with energy abundance and affordability. And we’ve been successful. If this [Invest in Tomorrow Coalition] becomes about going after Republicans and turns solar back into a partisan issue, that would be an epic blunder,” says Russell Gold, T1’s executive vice president for strategic communications.

Tom Matzzie, the chief executive of solar company CleanChoice Energy, is serving as executive chair of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC. Cofounders include Peter Davidson, CEO of the investment firm Aligned Climate Capital, and Michael Brune, former executive director of the Sierra Club. But it’s Larsen who supplied the lion’s share of the early money for the PAC—$6 million of the initial $7 million or so it had raised through August 31, according to federal election commission records.

He’s had an uneven record of political giving, of late. Earlier this year, Larsen spent $3.5 million to support congressional candidate Alex Bores, who was targeted by the AI industry and lost his race. Larsen’s company, Ripple Labs, has donated nearly $100 million to Fairshake, the pro-crypto PAC, which racked up electoral successes in 2024 but just lost a major fight when its preferred bill to regulate cryptocurrencies died in the Senate.

The willingness to go on the attack isn’t the only way that Larsen’s PAC differs from others in the green movement. Not that long ago, renewable advocates talked about an “energy transition” away from old, dirty fossil fuels and toward newer, cleaner ones. Larsen is suggesting instead to red-district politicians that they embrace the idea of fossil and renewable energy sources existing side-by-side, even as the PAC he funds throws haymakers at solar’s enemies.

“You could be pro oil and gas and pro solar,” he says.

entries.title: JackRabbit MG Cargo Bike Review (2026): Compact and Powerful
entries.summary: This compact, plucky ride is the cargo ebike for people who don’t want a cargo ebike. It’s even fun to ride.
entries.content:
JackRabbit is known for making lightweight, zippy, fun little scooter hybrids that physically resemble BMX trick bikes. I loved the easy mobility and high-speed capability of JackRabbit's equally powerful XG Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) when I tested that model last year. I'd worried that the MG Cargo—18 pounds heavier and nearly a foot longer than the XG—would compromise too much on these virtues. I needn't have worried. As I quickly learned, the pleasantly peppy MG rides like an off-road bike when you're not hauling a big load.

Its three throttle speeds max out at about 20 mph, 15 mph, and 7 mph, respectively. The lowest speed is manageable for a sidewalk, while the fastest hits top speed within about 50 feet on flat ground, unless you've got some weight behind (or on) you. The MG advertises a range of 48 miles, though I'll assume this requires being a lighter rider who is gentle on the throttle. As a 200-pound man with an admittedly heavy throttle thumb, I only made it to about 25 miles, even with minimal cargo. Because the bike's battery indicator shows up as at least half-full for the vast majority of this range, you'll need to test and learn your personal range when doing so is not mission-critical.

Note that because JackRabbits don't have working pedals, the bikes exist in an interesting technical gray area in some states in terms of their classification. Specifically, one could debate whether they're really a Class 2 ebike that can ride on bike lanes and trails. Given the MG's maximum speed of 20 mph—aside from an honor-system 24-mph jailbreak speed you can unlock for off-road riding—it mostly looks and quacks like a Class 2 ebike. In my experience, it's also treated as such.

The MG also offers nice customization options for accessorizing. It's easy to add a couple of rear pannier bags to the rear mounting rack or side racks ($75) on each side, offering enough capacity for most small grocery trips or beach excursions without adding much bulk. You could also opt for a rear basket.

entries.title: cool kids are writing in all lowercase now. does that make you mad?
entries.summary: a certain kind of person writes in all lowercase now. why?
entries.content:
the worst person you know probably writes in all lowercase.

they’ll tell you it’s an aesthetic choice, a testament to informality. they’re likely a twentysomething brooklyn resident like myself, bullish on being not the voice of their generation but a voice of a generation, and definitely guilty of posting performative notes-app screenshots and pseudointellectual, stream-of-consciousness “musings” that compare charli xcx to the pope.

what are they really up to, and do they know they’re participating in a long, exclusive, exclusionary tradition? the stylistic choice to write in lowercase is a dead horse that’s been beaten, flogged, and beaten again—what my generation calls ran through. and yet, it’s having a moment. i had to investigate.

for one side of the internet, lowercase writing is feminine.

it’s a “formal feature of how girls engage online,” says rayne fisher-quann, who’s 25 and lives (where else?) in brooklyn. known to the web for the all-lowercase personal essays she writes for her blog internet princess, fisher-quann insists that the offhandedness of lowercase “neutralizes” the self-importance of writing about oneself. it’s a way, fisher-quann says, “to avoid criticism.”

her feelings trace back to the digital spaces she occupied in her adolescence. “i got a lot of intellectual enrichment and influence from early 2010s feminist tumblr,” fisher-quann tells me. a decade-plus ago, incisive microblogs were on the rise on the platform, alongside the now-canonical page justgirlythings. justgirlythings pioneered the art of superimposing an all-lowercase serif-font sentence on a desaturated image (usually of a young woman wearing an oversized jumper and a messy bun sitting by a fireplace). it mostly covered cozy clichés such as “rainy days” and “lazy sundays.” becky campos, the blog’s author, says she wrote justgirlythings “because it almost felt like you were reading more of my diary instead of some polished copy. it showed that i’m more of a real person than some corporation making the posts.”

then there was rupi kaur, the instapoet of my generation. kaur’s work investigated the less manicured parts of the female experience, also through a lack of capitalization, except her words weren’t accompanied by stock imagery—they were the image. this performance of accessible vulnerability, akin to a live-laugh-love pillow, was kryptonite for millennial women: in 2016, kaur’s debut collection, milk and honey, sold more copies than the next-best-selling work of poetry, the odyssey, by a factor of 10. in homer’s defense, he didn’t have instagram.

while kaur describes her fixation on lowercase as an “ode to my identity as a diasporic punjabi sikh woman” (gurmukhi script only has one case) and a way to channel “equalness,” the virality of her work cemented the supple curves of the lowercase alphabet as an expression of femininity during the early days of social media. and the story might end there, if the internet were only populated by women.

but, to burst my own algorithmic bubble: behind every justgirlythings fan is a 4chan power user.

“i’m willing to believe that [using lowercase] is more deliberately aestheticized among young women on tumblr,” says adam aleksic, an internet linguist who goes by etymologynerd, “but none of the mega online communities use regular punctuation.” he and i are talking at a swanky coffee shop in soho, where he’s finishing up research on why the r-word is making a comeback.

to make his point, etymologynerd pulls up 4chan on his phone and starts scrolling. among the rancid all-lowercase musings, i notice a plethora of greater-than signs, angle brackets, and asterisks. because 4chan doesn’t support—has never supported—rich text (italicization, bolding, etc.), users also employ text-markup conventions: *yes* for yes, /i/hell no/i/ as hell no, etc.

while many may contend that writing in lowercase is a callback to one’s youth, sites like 4chan remind us that, at least within the digital sphere, the callback goes back much further and is part of a larger tradition. “lower case? it started with single-case tty model 33. now, it is habit,” ken thompson writes, in lowercase, in an email where he politely declines my request for an interview. (notice how thompson spells lower case as two words instead of one. before lowercase was a cornerstone of identity politics, it was just a lower case of the alphabet.)

ken thompson is 83 years old and, of course, one of the computer scientists to whom we owe the existence of the internet. he’s referring, in his email, to the teletype model 33, a popular terminal used for telecommunications that debuted in 1963. back in the ’50s, computers functioned on terminals that could support only 64 unique characters that—counting numbers, punctuation, and special characters—left no room for lowercase letters. this meant that most early programming languages (fortran, pascal, lisp) were written exclusively in uppercase. it was only between the ’60s and ’70s, when hardware manufacturing started to mature and memory costs started to plummet, that more characters became possible.

in early 1969, thompson got pulled from a project at bell labs, leaving him with nothing but time. so he decided to try to port a video game he had developed on company-owned equipment, space travel, to a more accessible pdp-7 computer he found unused in a neighboring department. he ended up reconfiguring the pdp-7’s operating system entirely and, alongside his colleagues dennis ritchie, douglas mcilroy, and bob morris, kickstarted the development of unix. unix made programming more ergonomic. with it, programmers no longer had to work with obscure machine code; there was no need to rewrite programs from scratch for every new computer model; and, perhaps most notably, it supported two cases.

soon, all the leading research institutions and corporations running on unix had to standardize how they capitalized in code: upper and lower case helped distinguish variables from constants (e.g., snake_case for variables, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants). these naming conventions, coupled with the increasingly collaborative culture of coding that unix established, evolved into a form of etiquette. capitalizing your code correctly was critical to how legible it was to other programmers, and excess capitalization was considered a faux pax. by the time this etiquette trickled down to the threaded text posts on usenet—the global network system created in 1979—the jargon file (better known as the hacker’s dictionary) had consecrated uppercase as SHOUTING.

point is, the internet used to be nerd country, reserved for those with technical expertise and written mostly in their idiom of programmatic lowercase shorthands. but everything changed in september 1993, when aol made usenet access a sign-on service, opening the floodgates to what the original usenet (then later irc and world wide web) users would call noobs. all of a sudden, an influx of digital non-natives started using proper grammar and correct capitalization, blissfully unaware of the rules that maintained the ecosystem they had just besieged. eventually, because there were just so many of them, the lowercase hacker vernacular became a marginalized quirk, and proper capitalization took over as the new norm.

i’m not saying the tumblr girlies stole from early-internet nerds destined for 4chan. but i am saying lowercase wasn’t invented by them, and perhaps has always been the hallmark of the outsider.

of course, maybe none of this matters. according to gretchen mcculloch, author of because internet: understanding the new rules of language, lowercase is a classic case of “resemanticization.” just look at something like “lol.” mcculloch’s theory is simple: first, a phrase is coined for a specific function (L.O.L. as laugh out loud). then, as more people use the phrase in different contexts (lol as an expression of nonchalance), its secondary meaning takes over. in just this way, the meaning of lowercase now bears no connection to its hacker associations, or even to its feminist co-optation.

today, lowercase can be clickbait—gong.io, an ai company that sells marketing data, analyzed over 85 million cold emails and concluded that those with lowercase subject lines get twice as many opens as properly capitalized ones do. i’ve heard of people my age who “become lowercase” because capital letters in texts and dating apps read as “too intense.” lowercase can also be a status symbol—when jack dorsey laid off 40 percent of his staff in february, he did so in an all-lowercase tweet. “the more senior you get, the less formal your emails are,” michelle liang, a tech growth investor, tells me. rarely were any of jeffrey epstein’s emails properly capitalized.

and yet, pockets of the internet still maintain that typing in lowercase is somehow antiestablishment, evident in the twitter trend of posting the phrase “i type in lowercase because i’m anticapitalist.” this could, perhaps, be a nod to the way writers like bell hooks used lowercase writing to “decenter” themselves from their writing; or to every college student’s favorite poet, e e cummings; or to the german bauhaus artists who deemed two cases aesthetically “inharmonic.”

aleksic, the etymologynerd, offers an alternative, more modern explanation: “people might be doing lowercase to signal that they’re not ai,” he says. obviously ai can write in lowercase, but you at least have to prompt it to do so, so there’s some inherent “friction,” etymologynerd says. after all, it’s not exactly easy to read an essay written entirely in lowercase.

the writer and self-diagnosed contrarian sam kriss sees beauty in how this tired, self-contradicting trope splits hairs: “writing enormous block paragraphs entirely in lowercase is the highest form of ‘respect’ i can render you,” he wrote recently on his substack. “reading my posts should be like scrubbing your eyeballs with sandpaper. i will keep attacking you until you are free.” etymologynerd goes so far as to insist that lowercase is the new normal.

or not. when i check back in on internet princess, fisher-quann’s substack, i notice she’s made a big change: she now writes with proper capitalization.

what say you?

entries.title: Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Review: Studio Quality
entries.summary: Nothing’s best headphones yet double down on design, comfort, sound quality, and highly adjustable EQ settings.
entries.content:
Outstanding sound quality. Premium build materials. Highly customizable EQ. Most comfortable Nothing headphones. Great ANC and transparency.

TIRED

Love-it or hate-it case. ANC is great, but not the best.

Nothing headphones have always stood out from the competition, and the Headphone (1) Pro is no different. It’s the brand’s most premium option yet, putting it up against the best from Sony, Bose, and Apple. After nearly a month of testing, I’d say these headphones belong among those top-tier choices, while bringing a few unique ideas to the table.

Exquisite Materials

Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Specs

Wireless connectivity

Bluetooth 6.1 with Multipoint, Auracast

Wired connectivity

USB-C (supports lossless up to 24 bit/192 kHz), 3.5-mm aux (supports lossless up to 24 bit/96 kHz)

Battery life

Up to 30 hours (ANC on), up to 68 hours (ANC off)

Weight

327 grams

Codec

LDAC, LC3, SBC, AAC

Water/dust resistance

IP52

Design is the first standout in the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro. On the outside, it follows the same formula as the Nothing Headphone (1) and Headphone (a), with a distinct square shape and two-tone, transparent outer shell.

The Headphone (1) Pro pushes this design to 11, largely by using premium materials instead of plastic. The square cans are made from a solid aluminum block. The arms are made of titanium. The transparent outer window is made of glass. There’s very little (if any) plastic to be found, yet they actually weigh 2 grams less than the Nothing Headphone (1).

The case is … interesting. It’s basically a hard-shell version of the purse-like case for the Apple AirPods Max 2—a near universally loathed case, I might add. The Headphone (1) Pro case offers better ear cup protection, but the headband remains exposed. It’s something you use once, then promptly forget.

All that being said, these are Nothing’s most comfortable headphones yet. The softer, thicker padding, wider headband, and reduced clamping force make these noticeably more comfortable than the Headphone (1).

Mixing It Up

Noise canceling and transparency are also great, thanks to extra microphones and impressive sound isolation. It’s not quite as bulletproof as Sony and Bose, but it was more than enough for any New York City situation I threw at it.

Inside, things get even more interesting. The headphone uses a triple-driver design—a bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver, and a treble xMEMS driver. The idea is that each driver handles a different frequency range, delivering clearer, fuller, less distorted sound. When every other major ANC headphone brand uses a single dynamic driver for the full frequency range, this triple-driver design is a big risk. Fortunately, sound quality is outstanding.

I’m not going to pretend I’m an audio engineer (I’m not). But songs I’ve listened to for years came back to life with the Headphone (1) Pro, with added emphasis, clarity, and energy in the midrange and treble I didn't expect.

I don’t usually make the stank-face to “Staring at the Sun,” by TV on the Radio, but I did pretty consistently with these headphones. Stevie Wonder’s “Another Star,” with its dense mix of vocals, hi-hat, trumpet, and guitar, sounded more spacious on the Nothing headphones than on the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). Bass is clear, but not as punchy as headphones like the Sony XM6. I didn’t mind, but it was a little less fun with artists like Bad Bunny and Kendrick Lamar, or anything in the EDM genre. A simple EQ adjustment changed this (more on that later).

This focus on engaging mids and highs meant that music on the Nothing headphones commanded my attention more often. I actually had a harder time achieving deep focus at work with these headphones than with more bass-forward mixes on the Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen.

That was a lot of sound talk, and everyone has different ears, different hearing, and different taste. Luckily, you don’t have to settle for one sound profile with these headphones.

The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro has some of the most customizable EQ settings I’ve ever seen in consumer ANC headphones.

First, there’s a physical “FLAT” switch tucked away on the left ear cup. When you turn it on, it changes to a neutral EQ designed for “reviewing music, producing, or mixing,” according to the brand. As someone who does none of those things, I still had a lot of fun using this mode. I even started to prefer Flat with certain songs and certain genres. One quirk: It increases the volume—I consistently had to lower the volume by two steps.

Second, the Nothing X app offers ample EQ settings. There are two EQ modes: simple, with a familiar three-band EQ (bass, mid, and treble), and advanced, where things get a little crazy. In advanced, you can dial in a +6 dB to -6 dB change for individual frequency bands on both the main driver and precision driver. This level of control is rare in consumer over-ear ANC headphones and will frankly overwhelm some people. That’s why I think more people will enjoy the Explore tab, where Nothing has curated five EQ presets to try out.

Add spatial audio modes on top of that, and you’ve got plenty of options to find your ideal EQ. Though I suspect many people will be happy with the sound out of the box.

Playing in the Big Leagues

The $400 price tag puts these headphones squarely in competition with the established, well-regarded $450 Sony WH-1000XM6, $450 Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen), and $550 (but always on sale for $450) Apple AirPods Pro Max 2. Those are three of the best ANC headphones you can buy.

I think the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro fit in that mix nicely. No, they don’t win in ANC or transparency performance (though both are solid). But it stands out with a unique design, tactile on-ear controls, an excellent sound profile, and in-depth EQ customization. It’s a toss-up whether I’ll use these or the Sony XM6 as my daily driver, and that’s high praise for Nothing's first take on premium over-ear headphones.

Harry Rabinowitz is a commerce editor at WIRED, where he covers headphones, earbuds, speakers, TVs, and fitness tech. Previously, he was the tech reporter at NBC Select, leading coverage and reviews of the same topics. Before that, he was a freelance writer for publications like Popular Science and Popular Mechanics. ... Read More

entries.title: I Ranked 28 Energy Drinks, From Celsius to Black Rifle (2026)
entries.summary: The future is here, and it is jacked up on B vitamins, red dye, and taurine. These are the best energy drinks to get from tired to wired.
entries.content:
Buying energy drinks in public is embarrassing. Every time I see someone scanning the cooler for their favorite flavor of Monster or Ghost, I guess which accompanying vape flavor they've picked out, and I know others are making the same assumption about me when I’m scoring a can of Celsius to beat back a hangover or get lifted before a 10-hour bartending shift.

The good news is that it’s easier than ever to purchase your favorite cans from Amazon, and the great news is that you don’t need to put on your Crocs and Cookie Monster jammies to do it. Throw in a nice little discount for buying in bulk and setting up auto-delivery, and you’re basically being paid to not leave your house. The future is here, and it is jacked up on B vitamins, red dye, and taurine.

As a devoted coffee drinker, I often feel like the misquoted New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael when I see neon-colored tallboys of high-octane energy drinks usurping shelf space from my favorite Dr. Pepper and Mountain Dew variants at my local Sheetz. Energy drinks are big business—they raked in close to $20 billion in the US in 2023—yet I don’t know a single person who drinks them on a regular basis.

A good cup of coffee is hard to find at odd hours in the middle of nowhere. Energy drinks, on the other hand, are as no-fuss as it gets. At any hour of the day you can pick out an eye-catching can that boldly advertises its caffeine content, plunk down a few bucks, and shoot into space in just a few swigs. Homebodies and deal junkies don’t even need to leave their domiciles to cop excellent deals with lightning-fast shipping on their most beloved brands, provided they’re Amazon Prime members. I love value, convenience, and caffeine, so I finally caved.

Still thirsty? Check out our other drink-related guides, including the Best Mushroom Coffee and Best Coffee Subscriptions.

Updated October 2026: We've added new drinks from Juno Energy and Kirkland Signature and a new flavor from Melting Forest, removed some discontinued products; and updated links, tasting notes, and prices throughout.

1. Celsius Functional Essential Energy Drink

Though it has less carbonation than most energy drinks, Celsius is punchy without a cloying aftertaste and it does wonders in masking the medicinal notes that are present in similarly potent drinks. This is an absolute unit when it comes to the caffeine-to-volume ratio, and not a single flavor I tried was objectively bad.

Celsius is a hot up-and-comer for a reason, and it’s not shocking to see entire fridges stocked with its whole portfolio right next to the checkout counter at a growing number of gas stations. The can has a whole lot of text I will never read, but it’s attractive and not too much in the extreme gaming or health-nut quackery camps to dissuade potential buyers who care about being seen in public with an energy drink. Like the Beatles or In-N-Out, this is a consensus pick everyone agrees on.

Notes: Nice mellow thrust of energy with very few jitters or butterflies in the stomach. This is a solid road trip or preworkout beverage. A slight dip in energy around 2 pm, but a few jumping jacks got me back on track.

Nutritional Stats (12 ounces)
200 milligrams caffeine
0 grams sugar
10 calories

2. C4

C4’s marketing materials position its sports fuel as the beverage of choice for the athleisure set. Does C4’s “clinically studied CarnoSyn beta-alanine” compound help you get swole? Do yoga pants increase flexibility? Who knows, and who cares! Halfway through the can I got happy feet and swapped my Aeron chair for the walking pad. Two miles and 35 minutes later I was still zooming, so I took my dog for a 2-mile run and felt like a million bucks at the end. I crushed a gas station salad for lunch and felt like a Healthy Person for one of the first times in my life.

Notes: With flavors like Frozen Bombsicle and Mango Foxtrot in C4’s arsenal, concerns of this “NSF-certified” drink tasting like saccharine gloop are valid, but the Midnight Cherry was a pleasant surprise. An intense cherry flavor—imagine a Dr. Brown’s dialed up to 11—hits on the frontend, and only a mild trace of diet flavor lingers in the aftertaste. Marketing be damned, you could add this to the rotation at a Taco Bell and no one would know (or care) about its alleged postgains powers.

Nutritional Stats (16 ounces)
200 milligrams caffeine
0 grams sugar
0 calories

3. Red Bull

Classic citrus flavor with minimal aftertaste and plenty of carbonation. That first sip brings back memories of all-night drives, marathon Excel sessions for the computer science class I took before I quit business school, and the countless “bomb” shots I consumed during this era. The gold standard for energy drinks. Minimal negative social baggage, maximal uplift.

Notes: The sugar high is sharp and abrasive, and the caffeine hits once the sugar wears off for stable energy well into the afternoon.

Nutritional Stats (12 ounces)
114 grams caffeine
38 grams sugar
60 calories

4. Naked

The realm of low- or no-calorie energy drinks offers two options for sweeteners: an unwieldy list of chemicals with confusing names, or allegedly “natural” options like stevia and monkfruit. The former camp commands the lion’s share of the market, but the latter is ascendant and willing to pay a premium for an energy drink with as few ingredients as possible. Naked’s entry in the field is our pick for the best of the woo-woo options that align more closely with yoga than gaming or deadlifting, and the few other options in this field aren’t even close as far as taste and firepower are concerned. Naked boasts just six ingredients, principal among them being fermented sugar and monkfruit. While we loved Jocko Go when it initially blazed the trail for monkfruit-based energy drinks, the mellow tang of Naked outclasses the sharp and astringent sweetness of the signature beverage of the wellness world’s favorite ex-Navy Seal/human-sized clenched fist.

Notes: Tastes like homemade lemonade boosted with just a hit of carbonation, with a barely noticeable “diet” finish that’s much easier to grow accustomed to than Jocko Go. It packs more than double the caffeine, making it a no-brainer when A/B-ing the two. The can is simple and devoid of aggro branding as well, which we’ll concede has no bearing on performance but is still a thing to consider if you’re worried about being seen slurping an energy drink in the office or at the gym.

Nutritional Stats (12 ounces)
200 milligrams caffeine
0 grams sugar
15 calories

5. Bloom Sparkling Energy

I never thought I would miss the flavor of old-school sugar-free energy drinks until I embarked upon this lifestyle. Monkfruit and Stevia certainly have their fans in the health and wellness space, but there’s something about the trashy delight of a fizzy, citrusy sucralose bomb of a sugar-free Red Bull that hits differently in this day and age. Gen Z’s endearing rebrand of Diet Coke as “fridge cigarettes” leads me to believe the kids love a little danger, and I’m not convinced a little hit of the S-word every now and then will kill me any faster than microplastics or the ambient thrum emitted by the data centers that are popping up all over my home state of Ohio.

Enter Bloom, which has all the aesthetics of a very-online wellness girlie product without any of the questionable flavors or adjuncts. Bloom’s 180 grams of green tea-derived caffeine does work during the early-afternoon doldrums, and the cute and crushable little can is one of the least offensive items one can be seen sipping on during an 8 am Zoom call or while commuting to the office. I still missed my morningly cup of coffee while I was trying this on for a week, but the tandem of caffeine and B vitamins tricked my brain into adopting a healthful effervescence that came in handy when a mountain of repetitive customer outreach tasks hit my inbox first thing on a Monday morning. This is a fun and friendly fizz-bomb that checks just about every box one may have when searching for a low-cal energy option that’s easy to find at just about any large chain store in the US.

Notes: The Juicy Orange flavor is dangerously close to the exaggerated citrusy sweetness of a Mountain Dew Kickstart—my personal favorite for hangovers and morning indulgence—all with none of the high fructose corn syrup and only one-sixth of the calories in a 12-ounce dose. The last few sips yielded a dry, almost prickly sensation against the back of my throat, but the flavor profile of Bloom is otherwise impeccable. Sucralose leads the charge on sweetness, with a modest dose of ginseng, lychee, green tea, and apple cider vinegar bringing up the rear. I did a double-take when I saw vinegar on the ingredients list, since the sip clocks in little to no bitterness to speak of.

Nutritional Stats (12 ounces)
180 milligrams caffeine
0 grams sugar
10 calories

6. Jocko Go

The manosphere is rife with snake oil merchants, and Jocko Willink is no exception. In addition to a MasterClass about leadership, the ex-Navy SEAL also hawks Jocko Go, a monkfruit-sweetened energy drink that makes highfalutin claims about “balanced energy,” “increased focus,” and “memory support.”

After just a few sips of this fizzy concoction I was overtaken by an urge to start a podcast about crypto and male decline. Instead of doing that I spiked the remainder of the can with a shot of Smirnoff and blasted off to the moon. I missed the memo that “bomb” drinks are out and borg-ing is in, but I have a strong feeling that Mr. Willink’s vitamin-rich riff on Turbo Fuel is sloshing around in gallon jugs at state colleges all across the land. It’s hard to tell where the caffeine ends and the 100 milligrams of B vitamins (more than 4,000 percent of the daily recommendation!) begin, but either way this tiny black can packs a wallop.

Notes: The flavor hits like a combo of Sunny D and stevia, which is an acquired taste for some.

Nutritional Stats (12 ounces)
95 milligrams caffeine
0 grams sugar
10 calories

7. Yerba Madre Yerba Mate

Due to its branding, lack of carbonation, and overall vibes, Yerba Madre (formerly Guayakí) is a caffeinated beverage that’s somehow exempt from being regarded as a capital-E Energy Drink by polite society. The stats on its cheery, GVC-inspired can say it contains no corn syrup or bizarre extracts—chemical or otherwise—and an absence of bubbles makes it dangerously chuggable compared to other drinks.

This is the caffeine vehicle of choice for liberal arts grads who spend their weekends wandering farmers markets with a hangover and a New Yorker tote filled with vegan junk food. You may not be able to dose a Mormon with one of these, but your “California sober” friend will gladly cut loose with a yerba mate while you take advantage of his offer to be the DD for the night.

Notes: The lack of bubbles is weird, but a hefty chug of one of these during a short break in Zoom meeting hell gave me just the boost I needed to draft (then delete) a subtly dickish email to a “cross-functional partner” about how they need to stop making Slack channels for everything. I finished the second half after work and was able to hustle through some household chores while still managing to crash by 10 pm—a win I never thought I would relish until I turned 40.

Others Tested

Ardor Tropical Mango (12-Pack) for $38: This is the best of all the Ardor flavors we tried, and it still tastes like someone rinsed out a glass that contained a mango White Claw with plain seltzer. It’s 99 percent flavorless. On the bright side, this may be drinkable if you have food poisoning and need to get caffeine in you without throwing up. Key Keytone Energy Drink Pineapple Passionfruit (12-Pack) for $45: Key is an “all natural” energy drink that’s very proud of its vegan and keto-friendly ingredients. It’s made with Avela, which is described as a “ketogenic ingredient intended for adult use” on its incredibly vague fitness-adjacent website. That’s all well and good if chasing ketosis is your hobby. If it’s not, you should run as far away from this beverage as possible. The initial hit of flavor is a muddled medley of faux-sweetness akin to woo-woo sugar replacements like Stevia or monkfruit, but what comes next is nowhere near as merciful. The astringent aftertaste hits somewhere between the final coat of goop your dental hygienist doles out and that last can of Mom Water that’s left in the cooler after a long day at the pool. The impact of so many foreign substances definitely had me feeling a certain kind of way within just a few minutes, but my attention swung wildly between work tasks, domestic minutiae, and creeping dread about our country's unraveling social fabric.

How I Tested

Across the span of a year, I sampled different energy drinks from an amalgamation of readily available gas station staples, brands the Amazon algorithm was pimping extra hard that day, everything in the Whole Foods end cap that advertised its caffeine content, and a couple oddballs from the past you probably don’t remember.

I graded on taste, which is obviously subjective, and the palpable effects of the caffeine after knocking back a can at 8:30 am every day, after my daily 1.5-mile run with my dog. The extra cans were deployed two hours into shifts at my part-time bartending gig. I took one day off from the experiment due to gut-wrenching stomach pain and horrible night sweats. If there’s a Ghost-addled gamer in your basement as you read this, please consider offering them a wellness check, or a refill on their tendies at the very least.
